items.title: Oura's TCX score replaces the survey with the conversation
items.dek: Oura built an LLM-based metric that reads every member interaction instead of asking members to rate it afterwards.
summary: Oura has built a total customer experience score (TCX) on large language models that evaluates nearly every member interaction across chatbot, live chat, email and phone.
The framework covers close to the entire base of more than five million ring wearers, rather than the small fraction who would have completed a survey.
Oura's VP of member experience frames it as closing a measurement gap that conventional CX tools left open once automation took over the front line.
items.why: Every Aldar line still scores itself on the opinions of the few residents, guests and students who answer a survey. TCX is a working blueprint for scoring the conversation itself, which would give Hospitality and PM & Leasing a read on the whole book rather than the vocal minority.
items.excerpt: "the best survey is the one you don't have to send" - Oura
items.oppText: Read every guest and resident interaction with an LLM and retire post-stay surveys on one line as a pilot.
keyInsights: Score the interaction that already happened rather than asking for a rating after it.
AI-read measurement covers the whole base, not the survey-answering minority.

items.title: Wellness is being delivered inside transactions customers already make
items.dek: Three unrelated operators added wellness to a purchase already happening, rather than building a separate wellness product.
summary: Three operators in different sectors attached wellness to an existing purchase: a hotel stay, a salon appointment and a supermarket's weekly promotional cycle.
The hotel case pairs W Melbourne with fitness app KIC, supplying in-room equipment, on-demand classes and a membership that continues after checkout.
The shared mechanism is distribution: the customer needs no new occasion, no new provider and no new booking.
items.why: The cheapest wellness proposition Aldar owns is the one attached to a stay, a lease renewal or a mall visit that is already happening. Hospitality has the strongest case, and the after-checkout membership is the part that turns a stay into a relationship.
items.excerpt: The mechanism these three share is distribution, not product.
items.oppText: Attach a post-checkout wellness membership to an Aldar hotel booking so the relationship continues past the folio.
keyInsights: Attach the new service to an existing transaction instead of creating a new occasion.
A membership that survives checkout converts a stay into a recurring relationship.
items.imageCredit: Paradisus Bali, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Eleven projects that widen what wellbeing means in built space
items.dek: Wellness has moved out of the spa and into residences, campuses and studios, on a scale that is now a specification question.
summary: A survey of eleven completed projects where wellbeing has moved beyond the spa into residences, campuses, fitness studios and healthcare space.
The set spans thermal bath resorts, longevity-focused residences, surf destinations and a university, a far broader definition than a hotel spa.
The piece cites the Global Wellness Institute's projection of a wellness economy approaching $10 trillion by 2029.
items.why: Longevity-focused residences are the direct read-across to Development. If wellbeing becomes a residential specification rather than an amenity, Aldar master plans need to price it now rather than retrofit it later.
items.excerpt: Wellness now reaches nearly every part of daily life, not just the treatment room.
items.oppText: Specify one Aldar residential release around measurable wellbeing outcomes rather than wellness facilities.
keyInsights: Wellbeing is becoming a building specification, not an amenity line.
Longevity-focused residences are the fastest-moving version of this for developers.

items.title: Dubai starts designing itself away from the car
items.dek: A new pedestrian and cycle bridge over Sheikh Zayed Road signals intent about the public realm rather than traffic relief.
summary: A 528-metre glass-sided pedestrian and cycle bridge now crosses Sheikh Zayed Road, part of a plan for 1,000km of cycle paths by 2030.
The writer found it nearly empty at dawn less than a month after opening, which is the honest early state of a new behaviour.
The piece reads the crossing as discretionary: the city did not have to build it, which says more about intent than about congestion.
items.why: New pedestrian infrastructure only earns its cost if arrival on foot is designed as an experience. Every Aldar destination sits at the end of one of these routes, and the last 200 metres are ours to design.
items.excerpt: The crossing was not strictly necessary, which is what makes it a statement about the public realm.
items.oppText: Treat the walking approach to one Aldar destination as a designed arrival sequence with shade, wayfinding and a welcome.
keyInsights: Pedestrian infrastructure creates an arrival experience that someone has to design.
Early low usage is a design and programming problem, not proof the route was wrong.
items.imageCredit: Vincent Eisfeld, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: An 866-hectare park gets a guest app built for the second visit
items.dek: Attractions.io built a visitor app for a Mexico City park holding nine museums, a castle and a zoo.
summary: Attractions.io has partnered with Bosque de Chapultepec on an app that helps visitors navigate an 866-hectare site.
At roughly three times the size of Central Park, the park is best treated as a collection of attractions needing several visits.
The app's job is planning across repeat visits rather than ticketing a single one.
items.why: Aldar destinations have the same problem: a portfolio of things to do and no tool that helps someone plan a second and third visit. This is a retention mechanic disguised as a map.
items.excerpt: A site this large is best approached as a collection of attractions rather than one visit.
items.oppText: Build one destination app that treats an Aldar site as a multi-visit itinerary rather than a single ticket.
keyInsights: Wayfinding tools are retention tools when a site is too big for one visit.
Plan the second visit inside the first one.

items.title: Baltimore turned an arts festival into a downtown strategy
items.dek: Moving the largest free arts festival in the United States downtown was a development thesis, not an event booking.
summary: Relocating Artscape into downtown Baltimore in 2025 became the centrepiece of Downtown Rise, a long-term strategy using culture to strengthen the central business district.
The approach traces to a 2022 ULI advisory panel that found the downtown had sound fundamentals but an inactive public realm.
Activation, development prioritisation and public safety were treated as one linked problem rather than three separate workstreams.
items.why: Aldar programmes events and develops districts on separate timelines. This is the case for writing a recurring cultural anchor into the development thesis for a district rather than marketing it afterwards.
items.excerpt: The festival move was positioned as a centrepiece of a long-term downtown strategy.
items.oppText: Commit one Aldar district to a recurring cultural anchor written into its development plan, not its marketing calendar.
keyInsights: A recurring cultural anchor can carry a district strategy if it is planned as infrastructure.
Activation, development sequencing and safety move together or not at all.
items.imageCredit: Kimberlyshorter, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Eight years and three billion chats inside Bank of America's Erica
items.dek: Bank of America's head of digital platforms on what three billion interactions taught the bank about personalisation.
summary: Bank of America's assistant Erica has passed eight years live and more than three billion interactions.
Jorge Camargo's argument is that the average customer does not exist, so personalisation has to be built per person rather than per segment.
The conversation covers scale, compliance and what generative AI changes about client expectations.
items.why: Eight years of a live assistant at that volume is the closest thing to a proven playbook for an Aldar resident or guest assistant, including the compliance work such a service would face under UAE PDPL.
items.excerpt: Camargo's position is that the average customer does not exist.
items.oppText: Scope an Aldar resident assistant around per-person history rather than segment rules, with retention and consent designed in from the start.
keyInsights: Segment-level personalisation stops being credible once you can model the individual.
Longevity, not launch, is what makes an assistant valuable: eight years of history is the asset.
items.imageCredit: MÁV Zrt., CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Airbnb makes a play for direct bookings
items.dek: Lower host fees, Google completing bookings inside AI Mode, and what direct booking now means.
summary: Airbnb is testing lower host fees on bookings that arrive through hosts' own links, roughly 6 to 10 per cent against a standard 15.5.
The booking still completes on Airbnb, which reopens the question of what direct actually means.
Google has begun completing hotel bookings inside AI Mode, and Delta is using AI-driven pricing to cut some fares by 20 to 40 per cent.
items.why: If the booking completes inside someone else's AI, Aldar Hospitality loses the arrival data and the pre-stay relationship at the same time. Direct has to be worth choosing, not just cheaper to supply.
items.excerpt: The booking still completes on the platform, which is what makes the direct question harder.
items.oppText: Make direct booking worth choosing with a pre-arrival benefit that only exists if the guest books with us.
keyInsights: Agentic booking moves the guest relationship upstream, away from the operator.
Fee cuts do not create a direct relationship on their own.

items.title: A residency is moving hotel demand like a sporting event
items.dek: Cultural anchors are shifting city hotel demand in patterns that used to belong to sport.
summary: Holiday-weekend demand data put cruise ports and national-park gateways at the top of the destination list, with the K-shaped spending gap narrowing.
A Madison Square Garden residency is moving New York hotel demand in a pattern closer to a major sporting event than a concert.
Generator's new chief executive makes the case for premium hostel product at around 40 pounds a bunk.
items.why: Cultural anchors move hotel demand the way sport does. Read alongside the Baltimore story, this argues Aldar's events calendar is a hospitality revenue instrument rather than a marketing one.
items.excerpt: The residency is shifting city demand on a scale usually associated with sport.
items.oppText: Plan one Aldar cultural residency explicitly against hotel occupancy targets rather than attendance targets.
keyInsights: Cultural programming is a demand lever with measurable hotel consequences.
Premium is a design and service claim, not a price point.

items.title: A 200-year-old brand rebuilds measurement for the AI era
items.dek: Clarks is rebuilding attribution as brand mentions start to displace clicks.
summary: AI is reshaping product discovery, so Clarks is rebuilding how it defines a marketing win.
Brand mentions are starting to displace clicks as the success metric.
Affiliate and attribution strategy is being rebuilt around a messier, less linear customer journey.
items.why: Aldar Retail measures by click and footfall attribution. If discovery moves into AI answers, mall and brand visibility stops being a search-ranking problem and becomes a citation problem.
items.excerpt: Brand mentions are beginning to matter more than clicks.
items.oppText: Track how Aldar retail destinations are cited inside AI answers, and treat that as a visibility metric alongside footfall.
keyInsights: When discovery happens inside an AI answer, citation replaces ranking.
Attribution models built on linear journeys stop describing reality.
items.imageCredit: CX Decoded by CMSWire — show artwork

items.title: What If AI Doesn't Fix Travel's Labor Problem?
items.dek: Travel's AI spend is aimed at office work while its labour crunch is on the front line — the two barely overlap.
summary: Rafat Ali argues the industry's assumption that AI will solve the hospitality labour shortage does not hold up against the data on where the shortage actually is.
The shortages are concentrated in housekeeping, kitchens and transportation — physical, front-line work — while AI investment is flowing to knowledge and office-based tasks with almost no overlap.

BLS data still shows roughly 941,000 open leisure and hospitality jobs and Skift Research puts average hospitality tenure at two years, so the demographic squeeze is structural, not a pandemic hangover.
items.why: Our Hospitality portfolio is exposed to the same front-line labour math. Investing in AI for back-office productivity is fine; assuming it fills a housekeeping or F&B shift is not — signature-moment experiences still need a named, retained human at the threshold.
items.excerpt: Ali frames the mismatch bluntly: front-line hospitality work is physical and ageing fastest, while AI investment is going almost everywhere else.
items.oppText: A visible, funded progression from housekeeping and F&B roles into supervisory and specialist tracks across our Hospitality operators, tied to a retention target rather than a headcount one.
keyInsights: AI investment and labour shortage sit in different parts of the operation — plan them separately.
Treat front-line retention, not just recruitment, as the operational metric that matters.
Signature guest moments depend on human continuity that current AI does not deliver.

items.title: Accor Is Bringing Movenpick and MGallery to India
items.dek: Nine months in, Accor's new South Asia CEO signals a wider brand play — Movenpick signed, MGallery imminent, The Hoxton opening in Bengaluru.
summary: Accor's South Asia CEO Ranju Alex confirms Movenpick has been signed for India and MGallery is on the verge of signing, with The Hoxton opening in Bengaluru in November and three to four further brands under review.
The move reframes India as ready for a diversified portfolio rather than the narrow upscale slice Accor has previously played, after two decades of slow traction in the market.
Only nine of Accor's 45 global brands operate in India today, so the announcement signals a step-change in brand density for one of Asia's most contested hospitality markets.
items.why: Direct read-across to Aldar Hospitality's international brand pipeline. When operators sequence four or five brands into a market they read as ready, the diversification decision is as much CX segmentation as it is real estate — worth mirroring in how we plan brand ladders on Yas and Saadiyat and any future international assets.
items.excerpt: Alex tells Skift the market has matured enough to absorb a much more diversified hospitality portfolio, calling the slate open.
items.oppText: A signature-moments map that separates the arrival ritual and service tone for each Aldar Hospitality brand tier, so we don't dilute across upscale and luxury in the same district.
keyInsights: Emerging-market brand plays now sequence four to five sub-brands, not one flagship.
Portfolio diversification in hospitality is a CX segmentation decision as much as a real-estate one.
Market readiness for upscale is a lagging signal — the operator that arrives with a brand ladder captures the widening middle.

items.title: Can Public/Private/Philanthropic Partnerships Unlock the Next Generation of Urban Industrial Development?
items.dek: Cleveland's Midline pilots a district-scale, self-recycling capital vehicle for brownfield readiness — a P3 with philanthropy sitting alongside.
summary: Cleveland's 350-acre Midline initiative brings together underused industrial parcels along a rail corridor and uses a purpose-built nonprofit — the Site Readiness for Good Jobs Fund — to prepare sites at district scale rather than one parcel at a time.

The fund was seeded with $50 million of the city's American Rescue Plan allocation plus roughly $25 million and counting from The Cleveland Foundation, and is designed to recover its investment through land sales, ground leases or equity so the capital recycles into the next site.

The article argues counties, not municipalities, hold the regional view that lets industrial corridors be re-assembled across jurisdictions, and reframes cities like Cleveland as pre-industrial rather than post-industrial.
items.why: Development. The P3-plus-philanthropy structure is directly transferable to how Aldar assembles adjacent parcels at masterplan scale — patient capital can carry the pre-development risk that no single project financing wants to hold, so operators arrive at a ready district rather than a raw site.
items.excerpt: The piece argues the future of industrial development may live inside legacy industrial districts, not on greenfield edges — provided someone underwrites district-scale readiness first.
items.oppText: A revolving, patient-capital vehicle that carries the pre-development risk on adjacent Aldar and partner parcels, recovering value on exit so the same capital funds the next district.
keyInsights: District-scale readiness beats parcel-by-parcel redevelopment when barriers cluster (environmental, ownership, infrastructure).
A self-recycling capital vehicle turns one-time public money into a permanent redevelopment engine.
Regional actors — counties, in this case — are structurally better positioned than cities to assemble multi-jurisdictional corridors.
items.imageCredit: Erik Drost, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Global Employee Engagement Continues Decline
items.dek: Engagement fell for the second straight year in 2025, and the sharpest drop is among the managers organisations rely on to land AI.
summary: Gallup's State of the Global Workplace shows global employee engagement declined for the second consecutive year in 2025, with South Asia posting the largest regional fall at five percentage points.
The steepest decline is among managers, historically the group with an engagement premium, which Gallup links partly to organisational flattening and larger spans of control.

The same body of research finds a direct manager championing AI is one of the strongest predictors of whether their employees actually use it — so engagement decline and AI rollout compound each other.
items.why: Corporate. Aldar's ability to land AI across the group runs through line managers. If we flatten spans of control to move faster on transformation, we may be draining the very tier we need as AI champions, blunting the investment in tooling.
items.excerpt: Gallup ties one percentage point of lost engagement to roughly 21 million fewer engaged employees globally, with a cited $10 trillion productivity cost.
items.oppText: Treat frontline-manager engagement as a leading indicator for AI deployment success across Aldar, and instrument it alongside AI usage metrics rather than in a separate HR dashboard.
keyInsights: Manager engagement is the operational lever behind employee AI adoption — it is not a soft metric.
Organisational flattening trades manager engagement for speed; the trade needs to be priced in.
South Asia's engagement decline is a signal for any Aldar operation drawing on that labour market.

items.title: U.S. Workers Continue to Report Downsizing
items.dek: Only 1% of laid-off workers name AI as the reason — but tech workers who barely use AI were three times as likely to be let go.
summary: About 21% of U.S. workers report their employer is letting people go, roughly steady across the first quarter of 2026 but well above pre-2022 levels, with federal government workers most exposed at nearly 38%.
Only 1% of currently laid-off workers name AI or automation as the primary cause when asked in their own words — most cite restructuring or cost-cutting, which may reflect AI indirectly.

Tech workers who used AI less than monthly were three times as likely to have been laid off as tech workers who used it at least monthly, so AI use looks like a resilience factor rather than a stated cause.
items.why: Corporate. Cuts against the reflexive 'AI is coming for jobs' framing and reframes AI adoption as personal resilience insurance for staff. Useful evidence base for how we position AI in internal communications and L&D investment across Aldar.
items.excerpt: Gallup finds AI shows up in the data not as the axe but as the seatbelt — regular users are demonstrably less exposed to layoff.
items.oppText: A group-wide minimum AI-use expectation tied to L&D rather than to performance management, using regular AI use as a workforce-readiness signal rather than a compliance metric.
keyInsights: AI use, not AI displacement, is the layoff signal visible in the data so far.
Framing AI adoption as personal resilience shifts the internal politics of rollout.
Non-adopters in high-adoption industries carry disproportionate layoff risk — a leading indicator worth watching internally.

items.title: Mapping the Busiest Year of CEO Turnover in Travel
items.dek: Skift Exec Search reads a dense cluster of eight CEO transitions and finds four patterns — including a hardening CCO-to-CEO pipeline.
summary: Skift Exec Search's inaugural quarterly Leadership Intelligence report catalogues an unusually dense stretch of CEO change across travel, from Accor's Bazin exit to Choice Hotels, Air Canada, Priceline and Turkish Airlines both promoting their CCO to the top job, and IndiGo importing Willie Walsh.
The report groups the transitions into four distinct patterns, including a hardening CCO-to-CEO pipeline and boards importing turnaround CEOs into high-growth markets.

It contrasts successful lifer CEO hires such as Capuano and Nassetta with failed ones such as Chapek and Linnartz, and flags Hilton's coming CTO hire as a market-rate setter for hospitality tech leadership.
items.why: Hospitality and Corporate. Signals where the sector is sourcing its next-generation leadership talent — commercial officers, not operators — which matters when Aldar Hospitality benchmarks its own succession pipelines against a shifting industry template.
items.excerpt: Skift Exec Search reads eight moves as four patterns, with the CCO-to-CEO pipeline hardening into a template rather than a coincidence.
items.oppText: Build CCO-adjacent commercial fluency into the Aldar Hospitality operator bench so the next generation of GM-to-CEO candidates carries it as a default rather than a bolt-on.
keyInsights: The CCO seat is now a live CEO pipeline in hospitality and travel.
Board choices in high-growth markets are increasingly imports, not internal promotions.
Hospitality tech leadership is about to reprice via the next round of C-suite hires.
